actual_facts.label: F8
actual_facts.text: [F8] $\pi$ and $D$ are probability measures; finite product sigma-algebras and finite products of probability measures are defined, the product measure has the rectangle formula, and Tonelli makes section integrals measurable and permits exchange of nonnegative product integrals. [[def-probability-measure]], [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

used_steps.claim: The fixed-predictor risks are defined by [F1], and the bounded product-measurable loss makes $R(\theta)$ measurable in $\theta$ by [F8]; finite projection, arithmetic, and Borel composition make $(\theta,S)\mapsto\exp(\lambda(R(\theta)-\widehat R_S(\theta)))$ product-measurable by [F11]. By [F14], this integrand lies between $e^{-\lambda C}>0$ and $e^{\lambda C}$. Thus $M_\lambda(S):=\mathbb E_{\theta\sim\pi}\exp(\lambda(R(\theta)-\widehat R_S(\theta)))$ is measurable, positive, and Tonelli [F8] exchanges the prior and sample integrals. Integrating step 1.1 over $\pi$ gives $\mathbb E_S M_\lambda(S)\le\exp(\lambda^2C^2/(8m))$.

actual_facts.label: F5
actual_facts.text: [F5] [[thm-kullback-leibler-is-nonnegative]]: under AC, $D(P\|R)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $P=R$, for probability measures with the first absolutely continuous with respect to the second.

used_steps.claim: Define $\alpha_k=N_k/n$, and for each subset $B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K\}$ set $P(B):=\sum_{k\in B}\alpha_k$ and $R(B):=\sum_{k\in B}\rho_k$. Finite sums make these set functions additive on disjoint subsets; a disjoint sequence has at most $K$ nonempty members, so they are countably additive. Step 1.1 and the candidate weight constraint give total mass one, hence [F3] makes $P,R$ probability measures. Each $\rho_k>0$, so $P\ll R$. For every subset $B$, $\sum_{k\in B}(\alpha_k/\rho_k)\rho_k=P(B)$, hence $dP/dR(k)=\alpha_k/\rho_k$. The KL definition [F4] therefore gives $D(P\|R)=\sum_k\alpha_k\log(\alpha_k/\rho_k)\ge0$ by [A1,F5]. The weight-dependent part of $Q$ at $\alpha$ minus that at $\rho$ is $\sum_kN_k\log(\alpha_k/\rho_k)=nD(P\|R)\ge0$, with equality only when $P=R$, hence $\rho_k=\alpha_k$ for every $k$ by [F5].

actual_facts.label: F3
actual_facts.text: [F3] [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]]: a latent-variable model supplies one jointly measurable nonnegative density on parameter, observation, and latent spaces, normalized on every parameter fibre; the observed marginal is its latent integral and the posterior is defined on positive finite marginal fibres.

used_steps.claim:
Define the complete-data density, relative to $
u$ times counting measure on $Z$, by $p(\eta,y,z):=\prod_{i=1}^n\pi_{z_i}\phi_p(y_i;\mu_{z_i},\Sigma_{z_i}).$ Repeated use of [F9] constructs the finite product measures, including $
u\otimes\#$, and preserves sigma-finiteness. AC supplies the countable-choice premise of [F11] by [F10]; repeated use of [F11] then identifies $
u=\lambda_p^{\otimes n}$ with Euclidean Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^{pn}$. For each component, [F1,F2] and finite-sum additivity [F18] give $\int f_\eta(y_i)\,\lambda_p(dy_i)=\sum_k\pi_k=1$. Distributing the finite sum over labels gives $\sum_{z\in Z}p(\eta,y,z)=\prod_i f_\eta(y_i)$. Repeated Tonelli integration [F12] therefore gives $\sum_{z\in Z}\int_Yp(\eta,y,z)\,
u(dy)=\int_Y\prod_i f_\eta(y_i)\,
u(dy)=\prod_i\int_{\mathbb R^p}f_\eta(y_i)\,\lambda_p(dy_i)=1.$ Thus $p$ is normalized on each parameter fibre as required by [F3].

For a fixed observed sample $x_{1:n}$, summing the complete density over the finite label set yields $m_\eta(x_{1:n})=\sum_{z\in Z}p(\eta,x_{1:n},z)=\prod_i\sum_k\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)=\prod_i f_\eta(x_i).$ Every factor is finite and strictly positive by [F1,F2], so this marginal is positive and finite. Its logarithm is exactly the likelihood $\ell(\eta;x_{1:n})$ in the statement. By [F4], every normalized posterior $q_\eta^{x_{1:n}}(z)=p(\eta,x_{1:n},z)/m_\eta(x_{1:n})$ is a probability mass function. More explicitly it is $q_\eta^{x_{1:n}}(z)=\prod_i\gamma_{i,z_i}(\eta),$ and every one of its finitely many masses is positive.

actual_facts.label: F3
actual_facts.text: [F3] A signed measure is a countably additive set function taking at most one infinite value; in particular a finite difference of finite measures is a finite signed measure. [[def-signed-measure]]

used_steps.claim: For each measurable $B$, $w=w_+-w_-$ and both integrals are finite, so $\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w d\mu=\alpha_\mu(B)-\beta_\mu(B)$. Countable additivity of both finite measures makes their difference countably additive with finite real values, hence a finite signed measure by [F3]. For every $B\in\mathcal T$ and every countable measurable partition $(B_j)$ of $B$, $\sum_j|h^1(\mu)(B_j)|\le\sum_j(\alpha_\mu(B_j)+\beta_\mu(B_j))=\alpha_\mu(B)+\beta_\mu(B)$; taking the supremum in [F4] proves the stated pointwise total-variation bound. The weighted penalty inequality follows by monotonicity of the nonnegative integral, first for simple nonnegative weights and then by increasing simple approximation. For a finite-valued simple $\varphi$, linearity [F5] and the definitions of $\alpha_\mu,\beta_\mu$ give $\int\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int w\varphi d\mu$. For general bounded measurable $\varphi$, choose $M$ with $|\varphi|\le M$ and partition $[-M,M]$ into finitely many intervals of length at most $1/n$; assigning one endpoint on each measurable inverse image gives a finite-valued simple $\varphi_n$ with $\|\varphi_n-\varphi\|_\infty\le1/n$. The errors in the two $\alpha_\mu,\beta_\mu$ integrals are at most $(\alpha_\mu(\Theta)+\beta_\mu(\Theta))/n$, and the error in the $w\varphi$ integral is at most $\int|w|d\mu/n$. Letting $n\to\infty$ proves the identity.

actual_facts.label: F1
actual_facts.text: [F1] For a nonnegative measurable $f$, the set function $B\mapsto\int_{\mathbb R\times B}f(w,\theta)d\mu$ is a measure. [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]

used_steps.claim: The coordinate $w$ is measurable, so $w_+$ and $w_-$ are nonnegative measurable functions. By [F1], $\alpha_\mu$ and $\beta_\mu$ are measures, and [F2] gives $\alpha_\mu(\Theta),\beta_\mu(\Theta)\le\int|w|d\mu<\infty$.

actual_facts.label: F1
actual_facts.text: [F1] For second-countable spaces with product topology, the Borel sigma-algebra on $X\times X$ equals $\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(X)$. [[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]]

used_steps.claim:
Each conditional probability measure in step 1.1 is sigma-finite because $X$ has mass one. If $X$ is compact, the Borel section-product construction in [F2] applied to the probabilities $\mu_i,
u_j$ on the full compact space $X$ gives a Borel product probability for each active pair; the cells themselves need not be compact. If $X$ is second-countable, [F1] and the ordinary product construction in [F2] give the same conclusion. Denote the chosen construction in either case by $\mu_i	imes
u_j$. Define $\gamma:=\sum_{i,j:p_i,q_j>0}\pi_{ij}(\mu_i	imes
u_j)$. Since zero rows and columns contribute zero by step 1.1, its total mass is $\sum_{i,j}\pi_{ij}=\sum_i p_i=1$. Thus $\gamma$ is a Borel probability measure.

actual_facts.label: F3
actual_facts.text: [F3] The Dirac set function is a probability measure, and integrating a nonnegative measurable function against it evaluates that function at the point. [[def-dirac-measure]] [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]] [[lem-dirac-integral-evaluation]]

used_steps.claim: By [F1], $X=[0,1]$ is a compact metric space, so [F2] applies. The point $(0,1)$ is Borel by [F5], and [F3] makes $\delta_{(0,1)}$ a Borel probability measure. Its coordinate marginals are $\delta_0$ and $\delta_1$, so it is admissible; [F3] gives its cost as $d(0,1)=1$. Thus $W_1^X(\mu,\nu)\le1$.

Let $h$ be any feasible real-valued function, so it is 1-Lipschitz and hence continuous and Borel measurable. Its parts $h^+=\max\{h,0\}$ and $h^-=\max\{-h,0\}$ are nonnegative measurable functions by [F4]. Applying [F3] to each part, for $c\in\{0,1\}$ we get $\int h^+\,d\delta_c=h^+(c)<\infty$ and $\int h^-\,d\delta_c=h^-(c)<\infty$. Thus [F4] makes $h$ integrable against both endpoint masses and gives $\int h\,d\delta_c=h^+(c)-h^-(c)=h(c)$. In particular, $f(x)=-x$ is feasible and has integrals $f(0)=0$ and $f(1)=-1$, so its objective is $1$. Every feasible $g$ has objective $g(0)-g(1)\le|g(0)-g(1)|\le1$, so the dual supremum is exactly $1$.

For any admissible coupling $\gamma$, the marginal conditions give $\gamma(\{0\}\times X)=1$ and $\gamma(X\times\{1\})=1$. The complement of their intersection has measure zero: each of the two complements is null, and finite subadditivity follows from the measure axioms [F6]. Their intersection is $\{(0,1)\}$. For any Borel $E$, if $(0,1)\in E$ then $\gamma(E)=1$, while if $(0,1)\notin E$ then $E$ lies in the null complement of that singleton, so $\gamma(E)=0$; hence $\gamma=\delta_{(0,1)}$. Therefore every admissible cost is $1$, and step 1.1 gives $W_1^X(\mu,\nu)=1$.

actual_facts.label: F1
actual_facts.text: [F1] [[def-finite-markov-decision-process]]: each joint row $p(\cdot,\cdot\mid s,a)$ is a probability mass function; $r(s,a)=\sum_{s',\rho}\rho p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$ and $P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_\rho p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$.

used_steps.claim: For each pair $(s,a)$, $P(s'\mid s,a)\ge0$ and $\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1$ by [F1]. Thus every true transition row is a probability law. The proposed $\hat P$ rows have this property by the Given condition. Since the spaces are finite and discrete, [F2] makes both transition tables probability kernels. The reward alphabet lies in $[0,1]$, so its probability-weighted finite sum $r(s,a)$ also lies in $[0,1]$, as does $\hat r(s,a)$ by assumption.
